items.prompt: Why does a foraging trail of ants fade away once the food source runs out?

options.label: Worker ants scrape the trail away once the food is gone
options.feedback: No ant patrols the trail to clean it. Nothing removes the scent on purpose.

options.label: The trail chemical is fixed to last a set time no matter what
options.feedback: If that were true, a busy trail and an abandoned one would fade at the same rate, and they do not.

options.label: Each passing ant adds a fresh trace, and with nobody walking it the scent simply evaporates
options.feedback: Correct — the trail is only as strong as its most recent footsteps.

options.label: The queen calls the workers back with a different scent
options.feedback: The queen stays deep in the nest; she has no way to reach or overwrite a trail out in the open.

items.ok_line: The path is rewritten by every ant that uses it.
items.ko_line: Ask what happens to a chemical that nobody keeps adding to.
items.exp_text: An ant that finds food touches its abdomen to the ground on the way home, leaving a chemical trace called a pheromone. Every ant that follows the same path lays a bit more, so the trail grows stronger as long as the food lasts. Once nobody walks it, the pheromone simply evaporates within minutes, and the path fades along with the food that made it worth marking.

items.prompt: What is the queen ant's job inside the colony?

options.label: She commands the workers where to dig
options.feedback: There is no central command. Workers act on scent trails and local cues, not on orders from the queen.

options.label: She lays the eggs that become every ant in the nest
options.feedback: Correct — production, not direction, is her role.

options.label: She guards the nest entrance
options.feedback: Guarding falls to workers built for it. The queen stays deep inside, rarely near an opening at all.

options.label: She forages for food once the workers are busy
options.feedback: It runs the other way: once a colony is established, the queen almost never leaves, and foraging is left entirely to her daughters.

items.ok_line: Every worker in the nest is her daughter.
items.ko_line: The queen's task is production, not the tasks that follow from it.
items.exp_text: A colony's workers are the queen's daughters, all sterile, and she is the only member able to produce fertilised eggs in large numbers. Fed and groomed by the workers around her, she spends her time laying, while every other task — digging, foraging, nursing the brood — is split among the daughters she keeps producing. The queen supplies the colony's growth; running the nest is left to everyone she made.

items.prompt: Why do leafcutter ants carry pieces of leaf into the nest instead of eating them?

options.label: The leaves are used to line the tunnel walls
options.feedback: The tunnel walls are bare soil. The leaves are put to a very different use once they reach the nest.

options.label: The ants chew the leaves into a paste that feeds a fungus they eat
options.feedback: Correct — the leaf is a farm input, not a meal.

options.label: The leaves attract insects the ants then hunt
options.feedback: Nothing is being lured. The leaf fragments never leave the ants' own tunnels for that purpose.

options.label: The leaves are stacked as a dry-season food reserve
options.feedback: The leaves themselves are indigestible to the ants; they are turned into compost for something else, not stored whole.

items.ok_line: The ants eat what the fungus becomes, not the leaf itself.
items.ko_line: Watch what happens to the leaf once it disappears underground.
items.exp_text: Leafcutter ants cannot digest the leaves they cut. Back in the nest, workers chew the fragments into a pulp, spread it on a spongy mat, and plant it with threads of a fungus that grows nowhere else. The fungus breaks the plant matter down and grows swollen tips that the ants harvest as food, so the leaf feeds the fungus, and the fungus feeds the colony.

items.prompt: Why do some ants stroke aphids gently with their antennae instead of eating them?

options.label: The stroking calms the aphids so they stop breeding
options.feedback: It works the opposite way: the ants want the aphids to keep feeding and multiplying, not to slow down.

options.label: It signals the aphid to release a drop of sweet honeydew, which the ant drinks
options.feedback: Correct — the tapping is a request for food, and the aphid pays it without harm.

options.label: It marks the aphid as prey for a later meal
options.feedback: A marked aphid is protected, not hunted, for as long as it keeps producing.

options.label: It cleans parasites off the aphid's body
options.feedback: The tapping targets the aphid's abdomen for a purpose tied to food, not hygiene.

items.ok_line: A tap of the antennae asks for a meal that costs the aphid nothing.
items.ko_line: An ant that wanted to eat the aphid would not keep tending it afterward.
items.exp_text: Aphids feed on plant sap and pass most of its sugar straight through as a sticky waste called honeydew. An ant taps an aphid's abdomen with its antennae, and the tapping triggers the aphid to release a droplet, which the ant drinks on the spot. In exchange the ants guard the aphids from predators and sometimes carry them to fresher shoots, tending the herd as a food supply worth protecting.

items.prompt: How do nearly blind army ants stay together while marching in a single dense column?

options.label: Each ant memorises the route from earlier trips
options.feedback: Army ants never nest in one place long enough to learn a route; they move to a new site every so often.

options.label: Ants at the front signal the ones behind with a call
options.feedback: Ants have no voice for this kind of signalling, so nothing is called back down the line.

options.label: Every ant follows the scent laid seconds earlier by the ants just ahead of it
options.feedback: Correct — the trail is remade continuously by the marchers themselves.

options.label: The column lines up along a fixed beam of sunlight
options.feedback: Columns move through leaf litter, under cover, and at night as well, so a beam of light cannot be steering them.

items.ok_line: Every ant is following a scent laid moments before.
items.ko_line: Army ants march in the dark just as readily as in daylight.
items.exp_title: Following a trail that is always fresh
items.exp_text: Army ants have poor eyesight, so the column is not held together by sight. Each ant lays a thread of scent as it walks, and the ants immediately behind follow that scent rather than any fixed path, keeping the whole mass moving as one dense ribbon. Because the trail is remade every few seconds by the ants currently walking it, the column can bend around an obstacle and close back up without anyone losing the way.

items.prompt: How does a tall termite mound keep its underground nest supplied with fresh air?

options.label: Termites fan the tunnels with their wings
options.feedback: Most termites inside the mound are wingless workers and soldiers; nothing beats air through by muscle.

options.label: The mound's chimney and porous walls set up a slow flow of air driven by temperature differences
options.feedback: Correct — the mound works like a chimney, without a single moving part.

options.label: Rain seeping through the walls pushes stale air out
options.feedback: Rain soaking the porous walls would clog them, not pump air through them.

options.label: The queen's breathing draws air down to her chamber
options.feedback: The scale is far too small; one insect's breathing cannot move air through a structure that size.

items.ok_line: Warm air rises and pulls cool air in behind it.
items.ko_line: Nothing inside the mound is big enough to move that much air by force.
items.exp_title: A mound that breathes without lungs
items.exp_text: A termite mound is built with a central chimney and thin, porous outer walls. Warm, stale air produced by the colony rises up through the chimney, while cooler outside air sinks back down through the porous walls to replace it. No termite pumps this flow; it runs on the temperature difference between the mound's core and its surface, turning the whole structure into a working chimney.

items.prompt: How can a termite get nourishment from wood, which is almost pure cellulose?

options.label: Its jaws grind the cellulose fine enough to become sugar
options.feedback: Chewing only breaks wood into smaller pieces; it does not chemically split cellulose apart.

options.label: Microorganisms living in the termite's gut break the cellulose down for it
options.feedback: Correct — the termite feeds a partnership it could not run alone.

options.label: Termites absorb sugar already dissolved in the wood
options.feedback: Wood holds almost no free sugar; nearly all of its energy is locked inside cellulose that first has to be broken apart.

options.label: Termites do not digest the wood; it only fills their stomach
options.feedback: Wood is genuinely eaten for energy, not carried as filler with no nutritional use.

items.ok_line: The termite supplies the wood; its gut guests supply the chemistry.
items.ko_line: Grinding wood into splinters is not the same as breaking its chemistry apart.
items.exp_title: A gut that is not working alone
items.exp_text: A termite's own body has no way to split the tough chains of cellulose that make up wood. Living inside its hindgut are protozoa and bacteria that do have the right chemistry, breaking the cellulose down into simple compounds the termite can absorb. In return the gut offers these microorganisms a warm, food-rich home, so the wood is digested by a partnership rather than by the termite on its own.

items.prompt: How does a single winged female ant start an entirely new colony after mating?

options.label: She carries a group of workers with her from the old nest
options.feedback: A founding queen leaves alone; no escort of workers travels with her on the nuptial flight.

options.label: She waits for workers to hatch from the old queen's eggs
options.feedback: Eggs laid by the old queen would only add to the old colony, not begin a separate one.

options.label: She keeps her wings in case she needs to fly back to the old nest
options.feedback: The wings are shed right after mating and never regrown, so there is no way back.

options.label: She breaks off her own wings, digs a small chamber, and raises her first workers alone on reserves stored in her body
options.feedback: Correct — she founds the colony single-handed before any worker exists to help her.

items.ok_line: One queen, sealed in, living off her own reserves.
items.ko_line: A founding queen has nobody with her when she lands.
items.exp_text: On her nuptial flight, a young queen mates with a male in the air, then lands and snaps off her own wings, since she will never fly again. She digs a small chamber, seals the entrance, and lays her first eggs, feeding the hatching larvae on reserves stored in her now-unused flight muscles. Only once this first brood of workers matures does she stop living off her own body and start running a colony.

items.prompt: What is one clear sign that a pale insect marching from a mound is a termite worker rather than an ant worker?

options.label: It has a narrow 'waist' pinching its body in two
options.feedback: A pinched waist is the mark of an ant; a termite's body stays broad and unpinched from front to back.

options.label: It is pale and could be either a male or a female
options.feedback: Correct — termite labour is not restricted to one sex the way it is in ants.

options.label: It has a hard, shiny black shell
options.feedback: That describes many ants. Termite workers are typically soft-bodied and pale, not hard and dark.

options.label: It carries a sting at the tip of its abdomen
options.feedback: Termites have no stinger at all; that trait belongs to certain ants and wasps instead.

items.ok_line: A cockroach ancestor explains the pale body and the missing pupa.
items.ko_line: Two insects can look alike and still not be close relatives.
items.exp_title: A relative of the cockroach, not the wasp
items.exp_text: Ants belong to the same insect group as bees and wasps, and their workers are always females with a pinched waist. Termites evolved from a cockroach-like ancestor and keep a cockroach trait ants lack: they grow through nymphs that gradually come to resemble the adult, without ever passing through a still, transformed pupa. Their pale, soft-bodied workers can also be either males or females, since termite duty is shared between the sexes rather than reserved for one.

items.prompt: How does a soldier termite defend a tunnel entrance against raiding ants?

options.label: It sprays a gas that travels far down the tunnel
options.feedback: Termite soldier defence works at close range, by blocking or biting, not by a gas that reaches far ahead.

options.label: It blocks the tunnel with its own oversized, armoured head
options.feedback: Correct — the soldier's body becomes the barrier itself.

options.label: It calls other soldiers with a loud chirp
options.feedback: No sound travels far enough underground for this; recruitment relies on chemical and vibration signals instead.

options.label: It changes colour to warn the colony of danger
options.feedback: A blind insect living in the dark cannot rely on a signal that has to be seen.

items.ok_line: The soldier's own head becomes the door.
items.ko_title: No gas, no colour, no call
items.ko_line: A blind insect underground has no way to use a signal that needs to be seen or heard from afar.
items.exp_title: A living plug in a narrow door
items.exp_text: Many termite soldiers have a head so wide and hard that it fits the tunnel like a plug, and when danger arrives that soldier turns to face outward and wedges its head into the opening, blocking the passage with its own armour. Ants attacking one at a time meet a wall of hard cuticle instead of an open door, and the soldier holds that position until the intruder is turned back or bitten by the mandibles guarding the gap behind it.
